citation: Sneha Tuli (Principal Product Manager, Microsoft), 'Enhancing Code Quality at Scale with AI-Powered Code Reviews', Engineering@Microsoft, 14 July 2025. https://devblogs.microsoft.com/engineering-at-microsoft/enhancing-code-quality-at-scale-with-ai-powered-code-reviews/
source_tier: Practitioner post (vendor corporate engineering blog, written by the product's PM)
access_status: Fully read via WebFetch (page text processed by a summarising model, so quotes are [uncertain] until checked against the raw page); search results also showed the post.
sponsor_and_incentive: Microsoft wrote it about its own internal tool built with the Developer Division Data & AI team. Microsoft sells GitHub Copilot code review, which the post says was informed by this work. Promotional tone, author works on the product.
exact_quotes: 'now has scaled to support over 90% of PRs across the company' (scale paragraph). 'impacting more than 600K pull requests per month' (scale paragraph). '5000 repositories onboarded to AI code reviewer observed 10 – 20% median PR completion time improvements' (results section). Basis: 'Per early experiments and data science studies.' 'In several cases, AI flagged bugs that might have been overlooked'. 'The author remains in control' (author applies suggestions by explicitly clicking 'apply change'). 'The adoption and impact of AI reviewer have been significant.' [uncertain: quotes relayed by fetch tool summariser, not verbatim-verified]
key_claims: An internal AI PR reviewer began as an experiment and now covers over 90% of Microsoft PRs, over 600K PRs a month. It posts PR summaries and review comments and suggested fixes, with a human in the loop. Claims faster PR completion, occasional bugs caught that humans might have missed, and positive reviewer feedback. Says lessons shaped GitHub's AI code review. Problem framing: PRs sometimes waited days or weeks to merge.
headline_figures: (1) 'over 90% of PRs across the company': adoption/coverage, matches lead. (2) 'more than 600K pull requests per month': the post says 600K, lead said 600,000, same figure; adoption, not outcome. (3) '10 – 20% median PR completion time improvements' for '5000 repositories onboarded': the only measured outcome, unit is median PR completion time, comparison group and baseline not stated, date unspecified (post dated July 2025), basis 'early experiments and data science studies'. Not in the user's lead as a number, lead only said 'accelerated review resolution'. No comment-acceptance rate, no adoption rate, no bug counts given.
sample_and_method: 5000 repositories for the completion-time figure. Method not described: no baseline, control group, period, or definition of completion time. Observational internal data, apparently company-run. Qualitative feedback described as direct from engineering teams, no survey numbers.
limitations: Stated: results described as from early experiments. Visible: no methodology, no control, self-selected onboarded repos (selection bias likely), 'median' hides distribution, no false-positive or comment-acceptance data, no quality outcome counts, no reviewer workload or fatigue measures, vendor author with commercial interest. Coverage and volume figures show adoption, not benefit.
what_a_leader_can_do: Supports the idea that leaders can deploy AI as first-pass reviewer at scale with a human approver kept in the loop. Evidence for benefit is weak: one unexplained 10-20% median completion-time figure. Does not show review quality improved or reviewer load fell. Honest reading: measured benefit is thin, mostly adoption.
overlap_with_site_essays: Light overlap with Checking Isn't Catching and The Verification Gap (AI review volume without measured catch rate). Touches What It Takes to Trust Agent Output (human stays in control, applies changes explicitly). Does not address Overseeing Agents Is the Tiring Part: reviewer fatigue not discussed.
